description: QuantumLC es un equipo de estudiantes del Liceo Científico Dr. Miguel Canela Lázaro con interés en la ciencia, la tecnología y la innovación. Nuestra participación en NASA Space Apps representa una oportunidad para aplicar conocimientos, fortalecer nuestras habilidades y trabajar de manera colaborativa en la solución de un desafío real.
summary: Listen to Earth is an interactive web platform that turns an official NASA aerosol visualization into sound. Starting from the GEOS Aerosols image (SVS 5669), it estimates the relative presence of dust, black carbon, sulfates and sea salt using non-negative decomposition of color. Each aerosol has its own instrument; intensity controls the pitch of the note and spatial coverage controls the volume. The platform offers three experiences: Dust Journey, Full Planet, and keyboard-based Manual Exploration, plus a direct lookup of the Dominican Republic. It works in Spanish and English, with no backend, accounts, keys or APIs at run time. We checked the method by comparing JavaScript against SciPy on 311 point samples and 870 sweep bands. In the image we analyzed, Saharan dust did not reach the Dominican Republic that day, and the platform lets you hear that as silence instead of forcing the result. The project addresses The Earth Information Jukebox by turning visual scientific information into a musical, interactive and more accessible experience, useful for education and outreach and designed also for people who are blind, have low vision, or learn better through sound.
details:
Earth science is almost always shown with maps and colors, which leaves out people who can't see them. We are students at Liceo Científico Dr. Miguel Canela Lázaro (Santiago, Dominican Republic) and built Listen to Earth so a NASA image can also be heard.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

The platform takes NASA's GEOS Aerosols visualization (SVS 5669, August 19, 2025) and generates sound from it live in the browser. For each region of the image, it separates the color into the four aerosols of the official legend (black carbon, dust, sea salt, sulfates) plus a silent neutral background, using non-negative least squares. Each aerosol plays as its own instrument on a 15-note pentatonic scale, so any value sounds harmonic. East-to-west position is time, relative intensity is pitch, and spatial coverage (the share of latitude bands where the aerosol appears) is volume. An aerosol sounds only if it passes three checks (weight ≥ 0.05, residual ≤ 10%, chromatic evidence ≥ 0.01); otherwise it stays silent.

There are three experiences: Dust Journey (30 steps, about 15 s, a tropical band from Africa to the longitude of the Dominican Republic), Full Planet (60 steps, about 30 s, 12 latitude bands per step) and Manual Exploration (an 8×12 grid of 96 positions; the R key jumps to the Dominican Republic).

ACCESSIBILITY

Everything works from the keyboard, with on-screen buttons as an alternative to the arrow keys. Every step and every grid cell has a text description exposed to assistive technology through live regions, and a table lists all 96 positions. Users control the volume of each instrument, the tempo (50–150%), mute and stop, and nothing plays until they start it. The interface is in Spanish and English.

VALIDITY AND HONESTY

We compared the browser's calculations with SciPy on 311 point samples and 870 sweep bands (scripts in the repository). The values are relative intensities read from an image of the whole air column, not µg/m³ or surface air quality, and the page says so. The sound stays faithful to the image even when that makes it quieter: in Dust Journey the dust fades out before the Caribbean (0.000 at the longitude of the Dominican Republic in this image), and the page says so and offers to play the sea salt that appears there instead.

CREATIVITY

Instead of giving each point its closest color, we decompose it, so a mix of dust and sea salt plays both instruments. A silent neutral background keeps gray land, ice and city lights from being heard as pollutants. An optional sustained layer that summarizes the whole image is inspired by NASA's Caldwell 73 sonification; no audio from it is reused.

IMPACT

It complements visual learning with listening, supports blind and low-vision users and learners who understand better by ear, and connects a global NASA dataset to something close to home: African dust crossing the Atlantic to the Caribbean. It is free, needs no installation or sign-up, and is shared with one link. The same method can be applied to other visualizations. Related SDGs: 4, 10 and 9, and as an educational contribution 3 and 13.

TOOLS AND AI USE

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; Tone.js 15.1.22 (bundled, no CDN); GitHub Pages; Python and Node only for verification. No backend, accounts, keys or APIs at run time. We used Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) to help with programming, data analysis and drafting. The team decided the approach, the sound rules and the scale, and reviewed every delivery. The audio is generated by code in the browser, not by an AI, and the page uses no AI while running.

DOCUMENTATION AND NEXT STEPS

Open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/dalgenisdalgenis-hue/listen-to-earth. The repository documents the method, sources and AI use (METODOLOGIA_SONIFICACION.md, SOURCES.md, AI_USAGE.md). The team tested controls and sounds on phone and computer. Next, we will test it with screen readers and volunteers.
